Q: How to show a letter by freetype-py within tkinter? A:

You usually don’t use freetype-py directly with tkinter. Because tkinter uses Tk’s built-in font system freetype-py is a low-level font rendering library, so it doesn’t plug directly into tkinter widgets.

You can use tkinter’s font system.

import tkinter as tk  
from tkinter import font  
  
root = tk.Tk()  
  
custom_font = font.Font(family="Arial", size=14, weight="bold")  
  
label = tk.Label(root, text="Hello", font=custom_font)  
label.pack()  
  
root.mainloop()

Q: How to get a password from a shell script without echoing A:

I wrote, for a script that create, format and mount a LUKS partition, a function that show stars in an interactive read substitution command.

getPass() { # getPass <prompt string> [variable name]
    local -i strpos=0 show=0
    local key subkey string=''
    while true; do
        if ((show)); then
            printf '\r%s %s\e[K\r\e[%dC' \
                   "$1" "$string" $((${#1}+1+strpos))
        else
            printf '\r%s %s\e[K\r\e[%dC' \
                   "$1" "${string//?/*}" $((${#1}+1+strpos))
        fi
        IFS= read -rsn1 -d '' key
        [[ $key == $'\e' ]] &&
            while IFS= read -d '' -rsn 1 -t .002 subkey; do
                key+=$subkey
            done
        case $key in
            $'\n' )                             # Return
                break
                ;;
            $'\E[D' )                           # Move Cursor Left
                strpos=' strpos < 1? 0: strpos-1 '
                ;;
            $'\E[C' )                           # Move Cursor Right
                strpos=" strpos >= ${#string} ? ${#string} : strpos +1 "
                ;;

            $'\177' )                           # Backspace
                ((strpos)) &&
                    string=${string:0: strpos -1 }${string: strpos } strpos+=-1
                ;;
            $'\E[3~' )                          # Delete
                ((strpos < ${#string} )) &&
                    string=${string:0: strpos }${string: strpos + 1 }
                ;;
            $'\E[H' | $'\001' )                 # Home or Ctrl+A
                strpos=0
                ;;
            $'\E[F' | $'\005' )                 # End or Ctrl+E
                strpos=${#string}
                ;;
            $'\EOP' | $'\E[19~' | $'\E[24~' )   # F1, F8 or F12
                show=1-show
                ;;
            *[!a-zA-Z0-9@#/\(\){}.+_\ éàöäü\!-]* )
                ;;
            * )
                string=${string::$strpos}$key${string:$strpos} strpos+=1
                ;;
        esac
    done
    echo
    printf -v "${2:-passWord}" '%s' "$string"
}

Bingings:

  • < Move cursor left,
  • > Move cursor right,
  • Home or Ctrl+a Move cursor at begin of string
  • End or Ctrl+e Move cursor at end of string
  • Delete Deléte one character under cursor
  • Backspace Delete back one character at left of cursor
  • F1, F9 or F12 Toggle string visibility (show current string instead of stars)
  • Return Validate user input and return string.

Syntax:

getPass <prompt string> [variable name]

Example:

getPass "Enter a new password: " pass1 &&
    getPass "Repeat same password: " pass2 &&
    if [[ $pass1 == "$pass2" ]]; then
        echo "password match!"
    else
        echo "password don't match"
    fi

Q: Search for a value in all tables in DataGrip A:

It is supported. In short, Ctrl + Shift + Alt + F (Windows/Linux) or Cmd + Option + Shift + F (macOS) should work. For detail, see https://www.jetbrains.com/help/datagrip/full-text-search-for-databases.html.

Q: Changing colors in a nested stochastic block model (graph-tool) to reflect higher-level communities A: 
import graph_tool.all as gt
import numpy as np
import os

g = gt.collection.data["celegansneural"]
state = gt.minimize_nested_blockmodel_dl(g)

# 1. Choose the level you want to use for coloring (e.g., level 1)
# Level 0 is the finest (individual nodes), higher levels are more aggregate.
target_level = 1 

# 2. Get the block partition at the target level projected to original vertices
# We transform the vertex membership into the labels of the 'target_level'
b_state = state.project_level(target_level)
b = b_state.get_blocks()

# 3. Use this projected property map for the colors
# Higher resolution and larger vertex sizes for better clarity
options = {
    'vertex_fill_color': b,
    'vertex_color': b,
    'vertex_size': 10,           # Increase this if the dots look like dust
    'edge_pen_width': 1.2,        # Makes the actual neural connections clearer
    'output_size': (1200, 1200),  # Higher res for better detail
    'bg_color': 'w',
    'output': 'hierarchy.png'
}

print("Drawing enhanced hierarchy to hierarchy.png...")
state.draw(beta=0.90, **options)
print("Done.")



'''
To modify the color scheme to reflect higher-level communities, the original code was updated with these changes:

* Level Projection: The core change was adding state.project_level(target_level).


* Replacing Static Colors with Property Maps: The fixed color arrays were replaced with the new projected map (b).


* Synchronizing Hierarchy and Vertex Colors: The options dictionary was expanded to include both the graph nodes and the hierarchy tree.

'''

Q: How to test the calling sequence of methods of a class? A:

To test the call order on an instance you can use the attach_mock feature. Calls to an attached mock will be recorded in the method_calls and mock_calls attributes of the parent mock. Then, since they're recorded on the same mock, you can explicitly make an assertion on the call order.

import unittest
from unittest import mock

from mount_manager import MountManager

class MountManagerTest(unittest.TestCase):

    def test_create_and_format(self):
        mount_manager = MountManager()
        parent_mock = mock.MagicMock()
        with mock.patch.object(MountManager, "create_file") as mock_create:
            with mock.patch.object(MountManager, "format_file") as mock_format:
                parent_mock.attach_mock(mock_create, "creator")
                parent_mock.attach_mock(mock_format, "formatter")
                mount_manager.create_and_format()
        parent_mock.assert_has_calls([mock.call.creator(), mock.call.formatter()])

This test should pass, given the mount_manager.py shown in the question.

However, if the order of create_file and format_file are switched in the implementation (i.e. in mount_manager.py) then the test should fail with an explanation looking something like this:

FAILED test_mount_manager.py::MountManagerTest::test_create_and_format - AssertionError: Calls not found.
Expected: [call.creator(), call.formatter()]
  Actual: [call.formatter(), call.creator()]
